title: Unisom and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Doxylamine Risks and Timing
excerpt: Can you take Unisom after drinking? How doxylamine and alcohol stack up as sedatives, how long to wait in each direction, who's most at risk, and the warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Can you take Unisom after drinking? How doxylamine and alcohol add up as sedatives, how long to wait, who's most at risk, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't take Unisom on a night you've been drinking. Unisom and alcohol both slow down your brain and nervous system, and together they add up. The result can be much heavier sedation than you expect, slower and shallower breathing, worse coordination, memory gaps, and a groggy, foggy next morning. The Unisom label itself says to avoid alcoholic drinks while using it. For a healthy adult, one tablet after a single drink is unlikely to be life-threatening, but there's no upside to the combination, and the risk climbs quickly with more drinks, higher doses, older age, or other sedating medicines.

**The quick rules:** If you've been drinking, skip the sleep aid that night. If you took Unisom, don't drink until it has clearly worn off, which for the classic tablets can mean most of the next day. Never drive or operate anything dangerous with both in your system. And if someone who drank heavily also took Unisom and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or confused, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how these drugs work and what the label says. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining Unisom with alcohol** or any other sedating medicine, and before using it if you're pregnant, over 65, have glaucoma, asthma or other breathing problems, trouble urinating, or take medicine for anxiety, pain, depression, or seizures. **Call 911 if** someone can't be woken up, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, has blue or gray lips, has a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious. For a possible overdose, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## How Unisom and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

The interaction between Unisom and alcohol isn't mainly about your liver or one drug changing how the other is broken down. It's about two sedatives landing on the same system at the same time. Doctors call this an **additive CNS depressant effect**, which simply means both drugs dial down your central nervous system (your brain and spinal cord), and the effects stack.

### What's actually in Unisom

"Unisom" is a brand, not a single drug, and that matters more than most people realize:

- **Unisom SleepTabs** (the classic blue tablets) contain **doxylamine succinate 25 mg**. Doxylamine is an older antihistamine and one of the most sedating ingredients sold over the counter.
- **Unisom SleepGels** and some other Unisom versions contain **diphenhydramine**, the same antihistamine found in Benadryl and ZzzQuil.
- Some Unisom "PM Pain" products pair diphenhydramine with a pain reliever such as **acetaminophen** (Tylenol), which brings a separate liver concern when you drink.

Always read the Drug Facts box on the exact box you have. The active ingredient is listed at the top.

### How the antihistamine makes you sleepy

Both doxylamine and diphenhydramine are **first-generation antihistamines**. They block histamine, a brain chemical that helps keep you awake and alert. Newer allergy drugs like Zyrtec and Claritin were designed to mostly stay out of the brain. The older ones cross easily, which is exactly why they knock you out.

They also block **acetylcholine**, a messenger involved in memory, attention, and many automatic body functions. This "anticholinergic" effect causes dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, trouble urinating, and, in some people, confusion. That last one is especially relevant in older adults.

### How alcohol makes you sleepy

Alcohol works mostly through different switches. It boosts **GABA**, the brain's main "slow down" signal, and dampens **glutamate**, one of its main "go" signals. The overall effect is sedation, slower reactions, and, at higher amounts, slowed breathing. (Our guide on [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy) goes deeper on this.)

### Why the combination is the problem

Unisom quiets the brain through histamine. Alcohol quiets it through GABA and glutamate. Different routes, same destination. When both are on board:

- **Sedation is deeper than either alone.** One drink plus one tablet can feel like several drinks.
- **Coordination and judgment drop further.** Falls, stumbles, and poor decisions become more likely.
- **Breathing can slow,** especially with heavy drinking or when other depressants (opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines, some muscle relaxants) are also involved.
- **Memory can get patchy.** Both drugs can affect forming new memories, so you may not remember the last part of the evening.
- **Anticholinergic side effects pile on.** Dry mouth, a racing heart, trouble peeing, and confusion can be worse, especially if you're dehydrated from drinking.

There's also a sneakier risk. If someone is very drunk, sedated, and lying on their back, their body's protective reflexes (like waking up and turning over to vomit) can be blunted. That's one reason heavy drinking plus any sleep aid is a genuinely bad mix.

## What the Unisom Label Says About Alcohol

You don't have to take anyone's word for this. The US Drug Facts label on Unisom SleepTabs tells you to **avoid alcoholic drinks** while using the product. It also says to ask a doctor or pharmacist before use if you're taking sedatives or tranquilizers, and warns that the product causes drowsiness and that you should be careful when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery.

The label also includes some other points worth knowing:

- It's meant for **occasional sleeplessness**, taken about 30 minutes before bed, once a day at most.
- It's **not for children under 12**.
- You're told to **ask a doctor first** if you have glaucoma, a breathing problem such as asthma, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis, or trouble urinating due to an enlarged prostate.
- If sleeplessness lasts continuously for **more than two weeks**, you're told to stop and see a doctor, because insomnia that persists can be a sign of another condition.

Diphenhydramine-based Unisom products carry similar warnings. None of them say "a little alcohol is fine." They say to avoid it.

## Doxylamine and Alcohol: Why the Long Half-Life Matters

Doxylamine deserves its own section because it behaves differently from diphenhydramine in one important way: it lasts a long time.

A drug's **half-life** is how long it takes your body to clear half of it. Studies of doxylamine in healthy adults have generally put its half-life at roughly **10 to 12 hours**, and it tends to be longer in older adults. In practical terms:

- If you take a tablet at 11 p.m., a meaningful amount can still be in your system the next morning, and some can linger into the afternoon.
- That's why many people feel a "Unisom hangover" (groggy, slow, foggy) the next day, even without any alcohol.
- It's also why the timing question works in **both directions**: drinking the next evening after a Unisom night isn't as clean a break as people assume.

Diphenhydramine has a somewhat shorter half-life in younger adults, but it's still long enough to cause next-day drowsiness in many people, and it also gets longer with age.

The takeaway isn't to panic about trace amounts. It's that "I took it last night, so I'm fine to drink today" is less true for Unisom than for many other medicines. If you still feel any grogginess, the drug is still doing something.

## Can You Take Unisom After Drinking?

This is the most common version of the question, and the honest answer is: **it's best not to.** Here's why it's tempting, and why it backfires.

### Why people reach for it

Alcohol often wrecks sleep. You fall asleep fast, then wake up at 3 or 4 a.m. with your heart pounding, too warm, and wide awake. That happens because your body is processing alcohol and bouncing back from its sedating effect partway through the night. (We cover this in detail in [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).) A sleep aid seems like a fix.

### Why it backfires

- **You're adding a sedative while alcohol is still in your blood.** At 3 a.m. after a big night, that's very likely the case.
- **Unisom doesn't fix alcohol-disrupted sleep quality.** Antihistamine sleep aids can make you unconscious, but there's no good evidence they restore the deep, restorative sleep alcohol interferes with.
- **The long action collides with your morning.** Doxylamine taken in the middle of the night may still be strongly active when you need to get up, work, or drive.
- **It makes the next day worse, not better.** You're stacking an antihistamine "hangover" on top of an alcohol hangover. Grogginess, dry mouth, headache, and slowed thinking all get worse.

### If you drank lightly

If you had one drink with dinner several hours ago and you're now sober, the risk is much lower than after a night out. Even so, the label says to avoid alcohol, and the safest choice is to ask your pharmacist about your specific situation rather than guessing.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take Unisom?

There is **no official waiting period** printed on the label or set by regulators, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours that applies to everyone is guessing. What we can say with confidence:

- **At a minimum, wait until the alcohol has fully cleared.** Your body processes roughly one standard drink per hour, but this varies a lot with body size, sex, food, and how fast you drank. After a heavy night, that can be well into the next morning.
- **By the time alcohol has cleared after a big night, it's usually morning.** That's not the time to take a sleeping pill that lasts most of a day.
- **So in practice, the answer for most people is: not that night.** Skip the sleep aid and use the non-drug steps later in this article.

## How Long After Taking Unisom Can You Drink?

The reverse question matters too, especially for people who use Unisom regularly or took it the night before a social event.

- With **doxylamine (SleepTabs)**, a long half-life means a good chunk of the drug can still be active the following day. A cautious approach is to avoid drinking until you feel completely back to normal and at least a full day has passed since your last dose. Your pharmacist can give you a more specific answer based on your age, health, and dose.
- With **diphenhydramine versions**, the effect wears off somewhat sooner in younger adults, but next-day drowsiness is still common.
- If you've been taking Unisom **every night**, don't plan on drinking without talking to a doctor or pharmacist first. Nightly use also isn't what the label intends, which is a separate conversation worth having.

## Unisom for a Hangover: Does It Help?

Some people take Unisom the morning after drinking to "sleep it off." There's no good evidence that it treats any hangover symptom, and it can make several of them worse:

- **Dry mouth and dehydration:** the anticholinergic effect dries you out further when you're already low on fluids.
- **Grogginess and slow thinking:** you'll likely feel foggier, not clearer.
- **Headache:** it does nothing for headache, and some people get headaches from antihistamines.
- **Nausea:** doxylamine is used in a prescription pregnancy-nausea medicine, which leads some people to assume it helps hangover nausea. It hasn't been studied for that, and combining it with leftover alcohol is the wrong way to find out.

If you're wiped out the next day, extra sleep can genuinely help, and our article on [whether sleep helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-sleep-help-a-hangover) explains why. But you don't need a sedative to get it. Rest, fluids, food, and time do more.

## Unisom SleepTabs vs. SleepGels With Alcohol

Because the brand covers more than one drug, it's worth comparing them side by side:

| Product type | Active ingredient | Alcohol concern |
|---|---|---|
| Unisom SleepTabs | Doxylamine succinate 25 mg | Additive sedation; long-lasting effect means next-day overlap is common |
| Unisom SleepGels and similar | Diphenhydramine | Additive sedation; same drug as Benadryl and ZzzQuil |
| Unisom PM Pain versions | Diphenhydramine plus a pain reliever such as acetaminophen | Additive sedation, plus the acetaminophen-and-alcohol liver concern |

None of these is "safe with alcohol." Doxylamine is often described as the more sedating of the two antihistamines, and it lasts longer, so if anything the classic tablets deserve the most caution after drinking.

If your product contains acetaminophen, read our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) too. Acetaminophen hides in many night-time products, and doubling up is a common way people accidentally take too much. If you're comparing other sleep products, our pages on [ZzzQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/zzzquil-and-alcohol) and [NyQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) cover those combinations.

## Unisom, Alcohol, and Pregnancy

Doxylamine has a second life as a pregnancy medicine. A prescription combination of doxylamine and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is used to treat nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, and some doctors suggest using over-the-counter Unisom SleepTabs with B6 for the same reason. That's why "Unisom" comes up so often in pregnancy forums.

If you're pregnant, the alcohol part of this question has a simpler answer: major medical bodies, including the CDC and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, say there is no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy. If you're using Unisom for morning sickness, follow your doctor's dosing exactly and avoid alcohol entirely. Also double-check which Unisom you bought, because the diphenhydramine versions are not the same as the doxylamine tablets doctors usually mean.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

The Unisom-and-alcohol combination is riskier if you:

- **Are over 65.** The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria lists first-generation antihistamines, including doxylamine and diphenhydramine, as potentially inappropriate for older adults because of confusion, falls, constipation, and urinary problems. Alcohol adds to every one of those.
- **Take other sedating medicines**, including opioid pain relievers, benzodiazepines (like alprazolam or lorazepam), prescription sleep drugs, some antidepressants, muscle relaxants, gabapentin or pregabalin, or other antihistamines. Several sedatives plus alcohol is where breathing problems become a real concern.
- **Have sleep apnea, asthma, COPD, or another breathing condition.** Anything that further relaxes breathing is a bad idea here.
- **Have glaucoma or an enlarged prostate.** The anticholinergic effect can make both worse.
- **Have to drive, work, or care for someone the next morning.** Next-day impairment from doxylamine is real even without alcohol.
- **Use Unisom most nights.** The body adapts to antihistamine sleep aids quickly, so they tend to work less well over time. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommended against using diphenhydramine for chronic insomnia. If you need help sleeping most nights, a doctor can help you find something that works better.

For a wider look at how common medications interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who have one drink and one tablet will just feel very sleepy. But this combination can go wrong, especially with heavier drinking, higher doses, or other medicines. Know the signs.

**Call 911 if someone who has been drinking and took Unisom:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, irregularly, or with long pauses
- Has blue, gray, or pale lips or fingertips
- Has a seizure
- Is vomiting while barely conscious
- Is very confused, agitated, or seeing things that aren't there

While you wait, keep them on their side (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit, and don't leave them alone to "sleep it off."

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if:**

- Someone took more Unisom than the label allows, with or without alcohol, even if they seem okay right now
- You're not sure how much they took or which product it was

Antihistamine overdose can cause a fast heartbeat, very dry hot skin, enlarged pupils, inability to urinate, confusion, and seizures. Large doxylamine overdoses have also been linked to serious muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis). These need medical care, not a wait-and-see approach.

**See a doctor soon if:** you regularly need a sleep aid after drinking, you find yourself drinking to fall asleep, or you notice shakiness, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you go without alcohol. Those can be signs that your body has adjusted to alcohol in a way worth checking with a professional.

## Better Ways to Sleep After a Night of Drinking

If you're searching "Unisom and alcohol," the real goal is usually just getting decent sleep after drinking. A few things genuinely help, and none of them involve stacking sedatives:

- **Stop drinking earlier.** Finishing your last drink a few hours before bed gives your body time to process some of the alcohol before you lie down, which tends to mean fewer 3 a.m. wake-ups.
- **Alternate with water and eat a real meal.** Slower drinking means a lower peak blood alcohol level and less disruption overnight.
- **Keep water by the bed.** If you wake up, rehydrate instead of reaching for a pill.
- **Keep the room cool and dark.** Alcohol can make you run warm and sleep lightly.
- **Accept a short night and nap later.** A 20 to 30 minute nap the next afternoon is a far better plan than a long-acting sedative at 3 a.m.
- **Save sleep aids for alcohol-free nights**, and only occasionally, as the label intends.

If you're curious about other sleep supplements, our article on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) covers that combination, and our deep dive on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains what alcohol does to sleep stages.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

Some people who drink socially take **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, on nights out. Here's a fair picture of what it is and isn't:

- **What the research suggests:** most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest DHM may affect how the body handles alcohol and how alcohol acts on GABA receptors in the brain. Human research is limited. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone.
- **What it is not:** DHM is not a sleep aid, and it does **not** make it safe to combine Unisom with alcohol. Because DHM appears to act on the same GABA system alcohol does, it's sensible to ask a pharmacist before using it alongside any sedating medicine.
- **Where it can fit:** as one part of a plan that already includes drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and hydrating. Some people use it instead of reaching for a sleep aid after drinking, not in addition to one.

If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Unisom and alcohol are both sedatives, and their effects add up: deeper drowsiness, worse coordination, patchy memory, and, at higher amounts, slowed breathing.
- The Unisom label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks. There's no safe "small amount" written anywhere on it.
- Unisom SleepTabs (doxylamine) last a long time, so the overlap can stretch into the next day in both directions.
- If you've been drinking, skip the sleep aid that night. If you took Unisom, wait until it has fully worn off before drinking.
- Be especially careful if you're over 65, pregnant, have breathing problems, or take other sedating medicines, and talk to your doctor or pharmacist about your situation.
- If someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or has a seizure, call 911. For a possible overdose, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take Unisom after drinking alcohol?**

It's best not to. Unisom and alcohol are both sedatives, and together they can cause much heavier drowsiness, poor coordination, memory gaps, and, with heavier drinking, slowed breathing. The Unisom label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks. If you've been drinking, skip the sleep aid that night, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have questions about your own situation.

**How long after drinking can I take Unisom?**

There's no official waiting period. At a minimum, wait until the alcohol has fully cleared, which is roughly one standard drink per hour but varies a lot from person to person. After a heavy night, that usually means the next morning, which isn't a sensible time to take a long-acting sleep aid. For most people, the practical answer is to skip Unisom on nights they drink.

**How long after taking Unisom can I drink alcohol?**

Unisom SleepTabs contain doxylamine, which has a half-life of roughly 10 to 12 hours in healthy adults and longer in older adults, so a meaningful amount can still be active the next day. A cautious approach is to avoid drinking until you feel completely back to normal and at least a full day has passed. Your pharmacist can give you a more specific answer for your age and health.

**What happens if you mix doxylamine and alcohol?**

Doxylamine blocks histamine in the brain and alcohol boosts the brain's GABA slow-down signal, so both push toward sedation and the effects add up. Common results are extreme drowsiness, dizziness, poor balance, confusion, and a heavy next-day hangover feeling. With heavy drinking, high doses, or other sedating medicines, breathing can slow dangerously. If someone can't be woken or is breathing slowly, call 911.

**Is Unisom stronger than Benadryl?**

Unisom SleepTabs use doxylamine, which is often described as more sedating than diphenhydramine (the drug in Benadryl) and lasts longer. Some Unisom products, such as SleepGels, actually contain diphenhydramine, the same drug as Benadryl. Either way, neither should be combined with alcohol. Check the Drug Facts label to see which one you have.

**Can I take Unisom for a hangover?**

There's no good evidence that Unisom treats any hangover symptom, and it can make dry mouth, grogginess, and slow thinking worse. If alcohol is still in your system, you're also stacking two sedatives. Rest, fluids, food, and time are better options, and a short nap later in the day is safer than a long-acting sleep aid.

**Is it safe to take Unisom with alcohol while pregnant?**

No. Doxylamine is sometimes used with vitamin B6 for morning sickness under a doctor's guidance, but health authorities such as the CDC and ACOG say there is no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy. If you're using Unisom for nausea, follow your doctor's instructions and avoid alcohol entirely.

**Can DHM make it safe to take Unisom after drinking?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the risks of combining a sedating antihistamine with alcohol. DHM's research is mostly from animal and lab studies, and because it appears to act on the brain's GABA system, it's sensible to check with a pharmacist before using it alongside any sedating medicine.
